episodes.212153: Deep moisture pooled across the lower Mid-Atlantic during the afternoon and evening of the 25th ahead of a slow-moving cold front situated near the Ohio River, with precipitable water values reaching into the 1.8 to 1.9 inch range across the Southside area of Virginia per Storm Prediction Center Meso-analysis. Abundant daytime heating allowed CAPE values to reach in excess of 1,500 J/kg during the evening. A line of slow-moving thunderstorms developed along a nearly-stationary surface trough that extended from Carroll County through central Halifax and Charlotte Counties, with multiple cells observed training along this boundary. The heaviest rain was observed within the Polecat Creek and Miry Creek basins, where nearly 5.5 inches fell within a 3-hour period. Multiple cells were estimated by radar to be producing rainfall rates of 3 to 5 inches per hour. Cells began to develop over the basins at around 6:00 pm EDT, with training reaching a maximum at around 8:00 pm EDT. Despite dry antecedent conditions with D3: Extreme Drought highlighted for all of Halifax County by the U.S. Drought Monitor, MRMS FLASH data estimated the rainfall reached the 200-year Average Recurrence Interval ceiling for a 3-hour duration along a east-west strip within the west-central portion of the county, with rainfall totals reaching 150 percent of the 3-hour Flash Flood Guidance. CREST Unit Streamflow ranged from 350 to 650 cfs per mi^2 during the storm.
episodes.212164: A decaying thunderstorm produced isolated wind damage in the northern portions of the city of Florence. Multiple rounds of heavy rainfall led to flash flooding in Marshall, Jackson, and Cullman Counties in Northeastern Alabama, flooding roads and causing them to become impassable.
episodes.212204: Scattered to numerous afternoon thunderstorm activity mainly focused along and east of the central mountain chain produced widespread gusty winds that lofted abundant dust from Albuquerque to Santa Fe May 25th. While the dust lowered visibility a couple of miles, severe outflow gusts reaching 63 mph were measured at the Santa Fe Airport.
episodes.212288: A few high-based showers and thunderstorms developed over southeast New Mexico during the evening of the 24th. One of these cells managed to produce a 61 mph wind gust at the Tatum mesonet.
episodes.212366: On May 25th, height falls ahead of an incoming trough and surface heating allowed for weak instability to build in across southwest Idaho. Strong south-southwesterly winds ahead of an incoming cold front allowed for a hot, well-mixed boundary layer and subsequent inverted-V temperature profiles. Shear was weak but sufficient to support a multicell with a damaging wind threat. Severe winds resulting in numerous trees down across the area.
episodes.212879: As high pressure wedged against the eastern face of the Appalachian mountains eroded, a warm front lifted north through southeast West Virginia. A passing mid-level shortwave trough contributed energy for the development of thunderstorms, with one storm becoming intense enough to produce damaging winds in Greenbrier County.
episodes.212891: A warm front was lifted into the area by a passing low on the 23rd of May, then the front stalled over central West Virginia and southwest Virginia through the 24th. Another low eventually pushed the boundary northward and then steered a cold front west to east across the area on the 25th.||Rounds of rain and thunderstorms traversed the area, with most robust activity occurring in the afternoon and evening of the 23rd and 24th. The majority of the area received one to three inches of rain during this time, with a few pockets between three and four inches.  Excessive rainfall flooded roads in Gilmer, Harrison, Lewis, Raleigh, Taylor, and Upshur Counties and led to a mud slide in Kanawha County. A couple of severe thunderstorms also produced damaging winds which downed trees and power lines in Logan and Mingo counties the evening of the 24th.
episodes.212892: A warm front was lifted into the area by a passing low on the 23rd of May, then the front stalled over central West Virginia and southwest Virginia through the 24th. Another low eventually pushed the boundary northward and then steered a cold front west to east across the area on the 25th.||Rounds of rain and thunderstorms traversed southeast Ohio, with most robust activity occurring  in the afternoon and evening hours of the 23rd and 24th. Much of southeast Ohio received one to two and a half inches of rain during this time, along with pockets of three to four and a half inch accumulations. Excessive rainfall flooded roads in Athens, Jackson, Perry, Morgan, Gallia, Meigs, and Lawrence counties and led to minor flooding on portions of Sunday Creek, Duck Creek, and the Little Muskingum.
episodes.213023: A stalled frontal boundary north of the region, as well as Gulf Coast and Atlantic Coast sea breezes, combined with usual early summer high instability and PWATs close to 2 inches to produce numerous showers and thunderstorms across the region, as well as isolated severe downbursts. Slow storm motion attributed to localized heavy rainfall and minor flooding.
episodes.213033: A similar environment to 5/24 took shape during the afternoon of 5/25, continuing into the late evening. Seasonal instability brought summertime pulse convection that was slow moving with efficient rain rates as PWAT's neared 2. This led to a couple instances of flash flooding in southern Lancaster County, SC early in the afternoon before bringing a couple more instances later in the evening near Augusta GA.
episodes.213064: A passing shortwave generated showers and thunderstorms across the upper Ohio Valley in the evening of the 24th. Some training of the storms resulted in higher amounts approaching 3 inches, which resulted in some isolated flash flooding in Ohio, West Virginia, and western Pennsylvania.
episodes.213210: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed on a daily basis across the region over Memorial Day weekend as a result of several passing upper level disturbances. Some storms produced severe hail, damaging winds, and flash flooding. Significant flash flooding occurred in North Richland Hills in Tarrant County on May 25th.
episodes.213260: Clusters of strong thunderstorms moved across the western coastal waters with reports of waterspouts and a measured wind gust of 43 knots.
episodes.213333: A midlevel shortwave lifted north through East Tennessee on May 24th, producing widespread showers and thunderstorms. Repeated bouts of heavy rain affected Knox and Loudon counties, producing some flash flooding in the South Knoxville and Loudon areas respectively. Additionally, a severe thunderstorm occurred in Hamilton County.
episodes.213382: A very moist air mass, with precipitable water values around twice the normal amount, combined with an upper disturbance resulted in a slow moving area of showers and thunderstorms that moved across parts of Sampson County in the afternoon. As much as two to three inches of rain fell in a short amount of time where training occurred, which was enough to cause some flash flooding in Clinton.
episodes.213385: A stationary front stalled across the Ohio Valley region during the morning, eventually lifting north in the evening hours. Showers and thunderstorms developed along this boundary with locally heavy rainfall.
episodes.213433: A fatality occurred when a man entered the Englewood Recreational Reservoir water and did not resurface.
episodes.213542: A trough moved through northern Arizona generating a few showers and thunderstorms.  One of the storms produced a landspout tornado in Apache County in eastern Arizona.
episodes.213570: Clusters of showers and thunderstorms affected the area for multiple days ahead of a cold front. Some storms were severe with impacts to trees and power lines.
episodes.213614: Scattered thunderstorms occurred ahead of a frontal boundary on May 23-25. However, on May 25, a mesoscale convective system developed west of the area and enhanced the low level wind field.  This resulted in two tornadoes across the tri-state area. One tornado affected the Villa Tasso area in Walton county in Florida, and the other tornado affected Houston and Henry counties in Alabama.  Both tornadoes were rated EF1.
episodes.213675: Heavy downpours occurred across central MS and south MS during the afternoon hours of May 25. These downpours lead to multiple roads to be flooded and one fatality.
episodes.213798: Widespread, slow-moving showers and storms trained over the same areas and resulted in locally heavy rainfall and scattered flash flooding across central and eastern Virginia on May 25.
episodes.213831: A weak midlevel low over eastern Texas and multiple mesoscale convective vortices maintained widespread convection along the central Gulf Coast on May 25th. Deep moisture and sufficient instability supported efficient rainfall as successive storms moved north and northeast over soils saturated by repeated rainfall during the previous several days. Flash flooding affected New Orleans from these storms.
episodes.213832: A weak midlevel low over eastern Texas and multiple mesoscale convective vortices maintained widespread convection along the central Gulf Coast on May 25th. Deep moisture and sufficient instability supported efficient rainfall as successive storms moved north and northeast over soils saturated by repeated rainfall during the previous several days. Flash flooding affected portions of Hancock and Pearl River Counties from these storms.
episodes.213833: A weak midlevel low over eastern Texas and multiple mesoscale convective vortices maintained widespread convection along the central Gulf Coast on May 25th. Deep moisture and sufficient instability supported a few severe thunderstorms. Stronger offshore storms produced severe marine wind gusts across portions of the local marine areas.
episodes.213960: A thunderstorm moved through the Tucson Metro on the late afternoon of May 24th. There was a recorded wind gust of 58 mph at KDMA with no reported property damage.
episodes.213962: A mesoscale convective vortex over Central Texas sent an outflow boundary into the conditionally unstable, moist airmass over South-Central Texas. This boundary generated thunderstorms that produced locally heavy rain leading to flash flooding.
episodes.214051: A weak upper low was located over southwest Arizona with southerly flow over the Rio Grande Valley.  This southerly flow helped draw up enough moisture for some high based thunderstorms to develop over the White Sands Missile Range and drop some strong wind gusts with them.
episodes.214086: Scattered thunderstorms developed across the northeast Georgia Piedmont during the afternoon and evening in association with a stalled front. One of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts in Elbert County.
episodes.214280: Scattered afternoon showers and thunderstorms formed, often producing strong outflow winds due to a dry lower atmosphere.
episodes.214404: A weak wave in northwest flow aloft enhanced the low-level jet into southeast South Dakota with moisture and better deep-layer shear arriving by late day near a weak frontal boundary.  With mixed-layer instability from 1500-2200 J/kg and marginally supportive deep layer shear of 40-45 kts, isolated supercells developed with mainly hail from stronger cells up to 2 inches in diameter.
episodes.214405: A weak wave in northwest flow aloft enhanced the low-level jet into southeast South Dakota with moisture and better deep-layer shear arriving by late day near a weak frontal boundary. With mixed-layer instability from 1500-2200 J/kg and marginally supportive deep layer shear of 40-45 kts, isolated supercells developed with mainly hail from stronger cells up to 2 inches in diameter.
episodes.214406: A weak wave in northwest flow aloft enhanced the low-level jet into southeast South Dakota with moisture and better deep-layer shear arriving by late day near a weak frontal boundary. With mixed-layer instability from 1500-2200 J/kg and marginally supportive deep layer shear of 40-45 kts, isolated supercells developed with mainly hail from stronger cells up to 2 inches in diameter.

Meteorologists from Arizona Public Service (APS) using two separate camera systems showed a landspout tornado on the ground for approximately 4 minutes.  Location is estimated.

A tornado moved ashore from the Choctawhatchee Bay into the small village of Villa Tasso. The tornado snapped and uprooted many hardwood trees, primarily on Yacht Club Drive, Robert Avenue, Magnolia Street and Virginia Court. Structural damage was largely due to fallen trees. However, one home on Hal Street suffered damage to about 40% of its roof. The tornado caused two trees to fall on a car at the intersection of Defuniak Street and CR 20 before lifting. Damage along most of the path was consistent with EF-1 damage with maximum winds estimated at 105 mph.
